files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller's checklist

Owner: C. Reyes. Complete in sequence; no shortcuts.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 that pays in July. If one exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities; note that in some months every payroll run pays in-month.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule, supporting contracts, and the GL. If it is absent, book June amortization as ONE combined journal entry; do not duplicate an entry already posted. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month each prepaid item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after checking the GL to confirm it has not already been recorded.
5. Test the expense coding on June vendor bills against the source documents and the GL. Reclass anything miscoded to the correct expense account.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, only after the entries and reviews in items 1-5 are complete.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Tidewater Outfitters began in 2018 when two longtime paddling friends noticed how difficult it was to buy dependable coastal gear without sorting through crowded catalogs and vague product descriptions. They started with a tightly edited online assortment and practical field notes drawn from weekends on bays, rivers, and marsh trails.

Today, the company sells outdoor apparel, dry bags, camp accessories, hydration gear, and compact equipment suited to day trips and casual expeditions. Its ecommerce storefront emphasizes plainspoken product guidance, responsive service, and useful bundles rather than an overwhelming range of nearly identical choices.

The team is small and hands-on. Merchandising staff regularly compare notes with customer support, warehouse colleagues flag packaging problems before they become patterns, and marketing favors trip ideas and how-to content over hard-sell copy. The group has a friendly, pragmatic culture, with plenty of debate about gear weight, weather resistance, and whether any meeting truly needs to be long.

Tidewater Outfitters remains an ordinary going concern. The current focus is on refining its product mix, improving fulfillment consistency, strengthening vendor coordination, and making repeat purchasing easier for customers. Management is also documenting routine processes so the business can keep growing without losing the knowledgeable, personal voice that shaped it.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction

Keep Tidewater Outfitters useful, approachable, and grounded in real trips. The brand refresh should sharpen the visual system and product language without making the company feel overly polished or corporate.

## Priorities

- Refresh core campaign templates, photography guidance, and storefront copy.
- Run two educational webinars per quarter, built around practical topics such as trip preparation, gear care, and choosing equipment for changing weather.
- Pilot a co-marketing program with a small group of complementary outdoor partners.
- Build seasonal content around checklists, field notes, staff picks, and customer questions.
- Improve post-purchase messaging with care tips and relevant product suggestions.

## Channel approach

Email will carry launches, field guides, and webinar follow-up. Social content should favor demonstrations, packing advice, and behind-the-scenes product testing. Paid media will support selected campaigns after creative and landing pages are validated. Partner activity should be limited to brands whose audience and service standards fit ours.

## Measurement

Review engagement, repeat visits, webinar participation, partner-sourced traffic, and conversion quality by channel. Capture lessons after each campaign and use them to shape the next quarter.

Budget remains pending Q2 close and channel review.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# Notes from your predecessor

C. Reyes — a few things that are easy to miss:

- The bank tends to place its own fees and charges near the end of the statement. We normally pick those up during close rather than booking them throughout the month.
- June moved fast, and some vendor-bill expense coding may be wrong. Check the source paperwork carefully; the documents in bills/ are authoritative, not the initial coding.
- The budget was fixed early in the quarter. The one-off June items were never planned, so they are usually the reason the larger budget-to-actual variances jump out.
- This month, the June 16-30 payroll run pays in the first days of July. The payroll register has the timing detail.
